section.title: God's Field and God's Temple
section.sectionRationale: Having shown that the gospel is God's wisdom received by the Spirit, Paul now diagnoses the Corinthians' factionalism as spiritual infancy. Their boasting in Paul or Apollos treats the servants as if they were the source. Paul overturns this with three images: the church is God's field where He alone gives the growth, God's building whose one foundation is Jesus Christ, and God's temple where the Spirit dwells. Every worker's labour will be tested by fire, and boasting in men is exposed as folly, for all things already belong to those who belong to Christ.
section.thesis: The quarrelling Corinthians are still worldly, but their leaders are only servants through whom God works; the church is God's field, God's building on the one foundation of Jesus Christ, and God's holy temple indwelt by the Spirit, so no one should boast in men when all things are already theirs in Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the Corinthians still worldly and quarrelling; God's field where He alone gives the growth; the one foundation of Christ, the building tested by fire, and the temple of the Spirit; and the folly of boasting in men when all things are yours in Christ.

units.label: Still infants
units.note: worldly, marked by jealousy and dissension

verses.text: Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly, as {{nepios|infants}} in Christ.
I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready,
for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man?
For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere men?

units.label: God's field
units.note: servants plant and water, but God gives the growth

verses.text: What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are {{diakonos|servants}} through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role.
I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.
So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow.
He who plants and he who waters are one in purpose, and each will be rewarded according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.

units.label: The one foundation and God's temple
units.note: Christ the foundation, the work tested by fire, the Spirit's dwelling

verses.text: By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds.
For no one can lay a {{themelios|foundation}} other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw,
his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work.
If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward.
If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.
Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s {{naos|temple}}, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.”
And again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”
Therefore, stop boasting in men. All things are yours,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you,
and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

nepios.gloss: An infant, a small child, one not yet able to speak or take solid food. Paul calls the Corinthians infants in Christ, not to deny their conversion but to expose their immaturity: their jealousy and party spirit show they are still feeding on milk when they should be growing toward maturity in Christ.

diakonos.gloss: A servant, minister, or attendant who carries out the will of another. Paul and Apollos are not rival masters to be followed but diakonoi, waiters at another's table, through whom the Corinthians came to believe. The word deflates all boasting in leaders: the servant is nothing, and God who gives the growth is everything.

themelios.gloss: A foundation, the base on which a building rests. There is only one foundation for the church, already laid, which is Jesus Christ Himself. No teacher may lay another; every builder must build on Him, and the value of each one's work will be tested against this fixed and finished foundation.

naos.gloss: The temple, specifically the inner sanctuary where God dwells, not merely the temple precincts. Astonishingly, Paul says the church together is God's naos and the Spirit dwells in it. What was once the holy of holies in Jerusalem is now the gathered people of God, holy and not to be destroyed by division.

basic.context: The Corinthians were splitting into fan clubs, 'I follow Paul,' 'I follow Apollos.' Paul says this proves they are still spiritual babies. He then reframes the whole thing with pictures: the church is a field, and God alone makes the seed grow; the church is a building, and its only foundation is Jesus; the church is God's temple, where His Spirit lives. Leaders are just servants and workers. One day every worker's labour will be tested by fire. So stop boasting in men, because in Christ everything already belongs to you.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul argues by images rather than abstract rules: field, building, temple. Each picture makes the same point from a different angle, that God is the true owner and worker, and the leaders are only His servants. The passage moves from diagnosis, you are worldly, to correction, God gives the growth, to warning, your work will be tested, to application, so stop boasting.
basic.originalLanguages: The Corinthians are nepioi, infants, still on milk. Paul and Apollos are diakonoi, servants who wait at God's table, not masters to follow. The church rests on one themelios, foundation, Jesus Christ, and no other can be laid. And the church together is God's naos, the inner sanctuary, where the Spirit dwells, so to wreck the church by division is to desecrate God's temple.
basic.typology: The temple where God dwelt among Israel now finds its fulfilment in the church, the living temple indwelt by the Spirit. The testing fire recalls the refining fire of God's judgment throughout Scripture, which purifies what is genuine and consumes what is worthless.
basic.christ: Jesus Christ is the one foundation, already laid, on which the whole church is built; no rival foundation can be set beside Him. He is the ground of all ministry and the one to whom the church belongs: you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God. All the treasures the Corinthians grasped at through their favourite teachers are already theirs because they are His.
basic.god: God is the true worker and owner: He gives the growth, He owns the field, the building, and the temple, and He dwells in His people by the Spirit. He is holy, so His temple is holy and must not be destroyed. He is just, testing each worker's labour by fire, and gracious, saving even the one whose work is burned up.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2 says the church is built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone. First Peter 2 calls believers living stones built into a spiritual house. Second Corinthians 6 says we are the temple of the living God. Isaiah 28 speaks of the tested cornerstone God lays in Zion.
basic.oneStory: God has always sought to dwell with His people, in Eden, the tabernacle, and the temple. Here that story reaches a new stage: through Christ the one foundation, God now makes His people themselves the temple where His Spirit lives. The whole Bible moves toward God dwelling with humanity, fulfilled in Christ and consummated when God dwells with His people forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 is the third and last panel of the long argument that opens at 1:10. Chapter 1 diagnosed the factions and set the cross against the world's wisdom. Chapter 2 explained how the Spirit gives the wisdom of the cross. Chapter 3 now brings the argument home to the Corinthians' own party slogans, and Paul does it in three movements: a rebuke in verses 1 to 4, a set of three pictures in verses 5 to 17, and a closing appeal in verses 18 to 23.

The three pictures are linked by a single thread. A field is planted and watered, verses 6 to 9. A building is begun on a foundation and built up, verses 9 to 15. A temple is indwelt and must not be destroyed, verses 16 and 17. Each image moves from the humble to the holy: a field is a place of work, a building is a place of lasting structure, and a temple is a place where God lives. Paul then shifts his picture at the very sentence where the images overlap. 'You are God's field, God's building,' verse 9, and 'you yourselves are God's temple,' verse 16.

The passage is also framed by two matching phrases. It opens with the Corinthians being 'mere men,' verse 4, and it closes with 'All things are yours,' verse 21, and 'you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God,' verse 23. The movement is from men to God, from a church that is measuring itself by human leaders to a church that sees itself owned by God.

Look at the repeated 'God's' too. In verses 9 and 16 and 17, God is the owner of the field, the building and the temple, and the possessive carries the argument. Paul's fellow workers are 'God's,' the field is 'God's,' the temple is 'God's,' and the Corinthians' favourite teachers are not theirs to own but theirs to receive. Verses 19 and 20 add two Old Testament quotations as a weight that holds the whole argument down.
context.historical:
This letter was written from Ephesus around AD 55, about three years after Paul left Corinth, 1 Corinthians 16:8. Paul had planted the church, Acts 18:1-11, and Apollos had followed him. Luke describes Apollos as a Jew from Alexandria, an eloquent man, 'well versed in the Scriptures,' who crossed over to Achaia and 'was a great help to those who by grace had believed,' Acts 18:24-27. It is easy to see how a church in a city that admired good speakers would divide into those who preferred Paul's founding work and those who preferred Apollos's polish. A third group claimed Cephas, which is the Aramaic name for Peter, and the BSB footnote on 3:22 says so, though Paul does not say that Peter had visited.

The images would have been immediately familiar. A Corinthian reader knew fields and crops, and the planter and the one who irrigates were different workers in an ordinary farm. The building trade was a visible part of a city rebuilt as a Roman colony. The materials of verse 12, gold, silver and precious stones on one side and wood, hay and straw on the other, would have recalled the way that wealthy buildings differed from poor ones. Anyone who had seen a fire in an ancient city, where cheap timber and thatch burned quickly and stone remained, knew what Paul meant by a Day that tests every work.

The temple image carried more weight than it does for a modern reader. Corinth was filled with pagan temples, among them the old temple of Apollo on a rise above the market. Jewish readers knew the Jerusalem temple, still standing in AD 55, with its cloud of glory at Solomon's dedication, 1 Kings 8:10-11, and its destruction by Babylon centuries before. To say that a gathering of ordinary people in a Greek port city was God's temple, and that God's Spirit lived among them, would have been astonishing. And to say that divisions could damage it was a grave charge.

The Corinthians' pride in their teachers also reflects a social pattern of the age. Students attached themselves to a favourite teacher and to his school, and a following was a mark of status. Paul takes that pattern and makes it ridiculous: he and Apollos are workers in the same field, not rival school heads.
context.canonical:
The three pictures each have deep Old Testament roots. Israel was God's field and vineyard. Isaiah 5:1-7 describes the LORD planting a vineyard and looking for fruit, and Jeremiah 2:21 speaks of Israel as a choice vine. When Paul says 'you are God's field,' he gives the church the title that belonged to Israel. The building image also has a history: 'I will build you up,' God promises in Jeremiah 24:6 and 31:4, and in Psalm 127:1 'Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain.' That verse sits close to Paul's claim that neither planter nor builder is anything, but only God.

The foundation of verse 11 recalls Isaiah 28:16, 'See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.' Paul's wording differs, but the logic is the same: God is the one who lays the foundation, and it is a person. The materials of gold, silver and precious stones echo the lists of materials for Solomon's temple, as in 1 Chronicles 29:2. And the fire has a long history, as the refiner's fire of Malachi 3:2-3 that purifies silver and gold, and Zechariah 3:2 with its 'firebrand snatched from the fire,' which is the nearest picture to the man who is saved 'only as if through the flames.' Amos 4:11 uses the same image.

The temple of God where God's Spirit dwells appears again in 2 Corinthians 6:16, where Paul quotes God's promise to dwell among His people and walk among them, and in 1 Corinthians 6:19, where the believer's body is the temple. Ephesians 2:20-22 combines foundation, cornerstone and temple in a single sentence, 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone.' Peter speaks of living stones being built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:4-5.

The two quotations in verses 19 and 20 come from Job 5:13, 'He catches the wise in their craftiness,' and Psalm 94:11, 'The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile.' The second is worth a glance: Paul changes 'man' into 'the wise' to point it at the Corinthians' pride, and the BSB's footnote marks the Psalm. Finally verses 21 to 23 anticipate Romans 8:32 and 8:38-39, where all things, life and death, things present and things to come, belong to those whom God has not spared His own Son for.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes as a pastor who has been told something painful. The Corinthians are lining up behind leaders and calling it spirituality. He wants them to hear that this is the opposite of spiritual. The word for it, in verse 3, is 'worldly,' and the proof he gives is behaviour, jealousy and dissension, not doctrine. A church can hold right beliefs and still show that it is walking 'in the way of man.'

He then moves quickly from diagnosis to rescue. The three images are not decoration. They are a series of reasons for giving up the slogans. If the church is a field, then no worker makes it grow. If it is a building on a laid foundation, then every builder is accountable to the one who laid it. If it is a temple, then it belongs to the God who lives in it, and what one does to the church one does to Him.

The warnings are real, and Paul means them to be heard by two groups. Teachers need to hear that their work will be tested. Church members need to hear that tearing the church apart is not a matter of taste. The final appeal, 'stop boasting in men,' is positive: they lose nothing by giving up their favourites, because 'all things are yours.' The whole passage is meant to move the Corinthians from clinging to leaders to resting in Christ.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The images describe what the church is, and the commands describe how to live as it. 'You are God's field' is a statement, not an instruction. 'Each one must be careful how he builds,' verse 10, is a command, and it is addressed to those who teach and build up the church, not to every member in the same way. 'Stop boasting in men,' verse 21, applies to every member.

The account of the fire in verses 12 to 15 describes what will happen at the Day, and it is sometimes taken as a recipe for rating other people's ministries. That is not its point. Paul says that each man's work will be tested, and testing belongs to God. The prescriptive force is to build carefully, not to inspect other builders.

Verse 17, 'If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him,' is a warning about a real danger, but it is not a rule for dealing with anyone whose ministry one dislikes. It is addressed to those who wreck the unity and holiness of the church through pride and division. It also needs to be read with the clear teaching that the believer is secure in Christ, Romans 8:38-39. Paul's concern is the seriousness of harming what God has made holy.

debates.question: What are the gold, silver and precious stones, and the wood, hay and straw, in verse 12?

views.label: Doctrine and teaching
views.case: The context is about teachers, and the foundation is Christ. So the materials are the quality of what teachers build on it, sound teaching versus shallow or false teaching. This is the view of many Reformed commentators, and it fits the surrounding argument about wisdom.

views.label: Converts, the people themselves
views.case: Since the building is the church and the church is made of people, the materials may be the believers brought in and how they were formed. Paul speaks in 2 Corinthians 3:2 of the Corinthians as his letter and in 1 Thessalonians 2:19 as his hope and joy. On this view good work produces genuine disciples and poor work produces nominal ones.

views.label: The whole of ministry, including motives and methods
views.case: Paul says the fire will test 'the quality of each man's work,' verse 13, and in 4:5 the Lord will expose the motives of the heart. This wider reading includes teaching, methods, character and motives.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the main claim stands: only what accords with Christ the foundation lasts, and the test belongs to God. Readers who press for one specific meaning should remember that Paul gives only the images and does not interpret them.

debates.question: Is the temple of verses 16 and 17 the church together or each believer?

views.label: The community
views.case: 'You' in verses 16 and 17 is plural in Greek, and the singular 'temple' is the group. The BSB footnote notes that 'in you' can read 'among you.' The context is a divided church, and the damage Paul warns against is done by division.

views.label: Each believer
views.case: In 6:19 Paul says that your body, singular, is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Some readers see verse 16 as anticipating that, with the Spirit dwelling in each person.

debates.bearing: The plural address and the context strongly favour the community here, and 6:19 applies the same truth to the body. The two readings do not conflict, since each believer shares in the temple, but the application in chapter 3 is to the unity and holiness of the church.

debates.question: What does 'saved, but only as if through the flames' say about purgatory and rewards?

views.label: A true believer who loses reward
views.case: The worker himself 'will be saved,' while his work is burned. The picture is of a man escaping a burning house with nothing in his hands, and the loss concerns reward, not salvation. Most Protestant readers hold this.

views.label: A purifying fire after death
views.case: Roman Catholic tradition has appealed to the passage, with other texts, in support of purgatory, taking the fire as a process of purification for those saved but not yet clean.

views.label: The fire tests works, not persons
views.case: A frequent reply is that the fire in the text acts on the work, not on the worker, and that the loss is the work's, so the text describes assessment, not a place of purifying.

debates.bearing: The text says the work is tested and the worker saved. It affirms that service matters to God and that salvation rests on Christ alone, which is why the foundation in verse 11 is the only one that cannot be replaced.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 1 and 3 use two related words that the BSB renders with the same English. In verse 1 Paul calls the Corinthians sarkinoi, 'of flesh,' and in verse 3 sarkikoi, 'fleshly.' Both come from sarx, flesh. Some readers press the difference, taking the first to mean made of flesh, as all humans are, and the second to mean governed by the flesh. Others think the two words are used loosely. In either case, the Corinthians' trouble is that they are behaving as if the Spirit were absent. The phrase in verse 3, 'walking in the way of man,' is literally 'walking according to man,' the same ordinary human standard that Paul contrasts with the Spirit in 2:14.

The image in verse 6 depends on the tenses. 'I planted' and 'Apollos watered' are in the aorist, a single completed act. 'God made it grow' is in the imperfect, which describes continuing action. Paul and Apollos did their parts at particular times, but God has been giving growth the whole time. The two workers come and go, and the growth is God's, always.

In verse 8, the BSB's 'one in purpose' is literally 'are one,' as the footnote observes. The planter and the waterer are a single thing, not competitors. Verse 9 calls Paul and Apollos 'God's fellow workers.' The Greek is theou synergoi, and the genitive is flexible. It can mean fellow workers who belong to God, or fellow workers with God. The context, with 'one' in the previous verse, leans toward 'fellow workers under God, with each other,' but the other reading is not ruled out. Either way the field and the building belong to God.

In verse 10 Paul calls himself an 'expert builder.' The Greek, sophos architekton, is literally a wise master builder, and the word 'architect' comes from it. It is a deliberate echo of the argument about wisdom. The only wisdom Paul claims is the skill to lay the right foundation.

In verse 13 the 'prove' of 'the fire will prove the quality of each man's work' is dokimazo, the verb used for testing metal and for approving what passes. Peter uses the same family of words when he speaks of faith 'refined by fire,' 1 Peter 1:7. In verse 15 Paul says the man will 'suffer loss,' zemioo, which is the language of financial forfeit, and the contrast with 'reward' in verse 14 is the contrast between gaining and forfeiting.

Verse 17 uses the same verb twice, phtheiro, to ruin or corrupt: 'If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him.' The balance is exact, a loss for a loss. And the 'temple' of verses 16 and 17 is naos, the inner sanctuary, not the courts around it, which would be hieron. Finally, verse 18 'become a fool' uses moros, the root of 'moron,' the same word as in 1:25 and 1:27 for God's foolishness and the foolish things He chooses.

typology.type: The church as the new temple
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle and the temple were the places where God's glory dwelt among Israel, Exodus 40:34-35 and 1 Kings 8:10-11. Paul says that the community of believers is now God's naos and that God's Spirit dwells among them. The correspondence is the dwelling of God with a people in holiness, and the warning of verse 17 matches the old rule that unclean or careless handling of the sanctuary was punished. The escalation is that God no longer lives in a building made of stone but in people, and the nations are being built into it, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short in that the earthly temple could be destroyed by armies, while the church, built on Christ, will not be.

typology.type: The foundation stone laid in Zion
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation, laid by God in Zion. Paul says the foundation 'already laid' is Jesus Christ. The correspondence is that God lays it and the believer rests on it. The escalation is in the identity: what Isaiah left as a stone, Paul names as a person, and Peter, quoting Isaiah, applies it to Christ, 1 Peter 2:4-6. The type is not complete until the final building is finished, when the one who believes 'will never be shaken' in the fullest sense.

typology.type: The refiner's fire of the Day
typology.fulfillment: Malachi 3:2-3 describes the Lord coming like a refiner's fire that purifies silver and gold. In Paul the Day brings every work to light and the fire proves it. The correspondence is that fire does not create value but reveals what is already there, consuming straw and leaving gold. In the New Testament the Day is the day of Christ's return, and Peter says that faith is tested by fire, 1 Peter 1:7. The picture goes beyond Malachi because it is applied to the work of each Christian builder, with salvation secure and reward at stake. It falls short of a full picture of judgment, since Paul speaks only of believers' work here.

typology.type: The firebrand snatched from the fire
typology.fulfillment: In Zechariah 3:2 the high priest Joshua is called a firebrand snatched from the fire, a man rescued from the judgment that fell on Jerusalem. Paul's man who is saved 'only as if through the flames' is in a similar position: he escapes, but only just. The correspondence is rescue by God's choice and not by merit. The escalation is that in Zechariah the rescue is followed by new clothes and cleansing, Zechariah 3:4-5, and for the believer in Christ the clothing is Christ's righteousness. The type falls short in that Paul does not say the man is cleansed in the fire, only that he is saved.

study.christ:
Paul puts Christ at the foundation of the church in a single clause, 'which is Jesus Christ,' verse 11. Everything else in the passage depends on it. The picture is not of a foundation that was Christ's teaching or example, though they matter, but of the person Himself, laid by God. The phrase 'already laid' shows that the foundation does not depend on anyone's building. Paul laid it in preaching, but the foundation is Christ's cross and resurrection, as he says in 15:3-4. A church can add to it and can even build badly on it, but it cannot change it.

Because Christ is the foundation, He is also the standard. The test of the Day is, in effect, a test of how work stands in relation to Him. This is why Paul can say that Apollos and he are nothing. The sum of Christian ministry is to serve a person who has already done what matters. The Day is the day of Christ's coming, 1:8, and the fire is His judgment of the work done in His name. It is also why the passage can speak of rewards without any shadow of earning salvation: the builder who sees his work burn is still saved, because the foundation holds.

The temple also leads to Christ. In John 2:19-21 Jesus speaks of His body as the temple that will be raised, and the church is His body, 12:27. The Spirit who dwells in the church is the Spirit of Christ. Paul's argument is that the church is God's temple because the one in whom God's fullness dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9, has joined her to Himself. The warning against destroying the temple is a warning against harming those whom Christ has made His own.

The last sentences describe a chain of belonging: 'you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God,' verse 23. The Son's belonging to the Father is not a slight to His deity. In the context of the argument it describes the order of the saving work, in which the Son carries out the Father's purpose. The Corinthians' idea of owning a teacher is turned upside down. They own nothing, and they are owned by the one who owns everything. The passage also tells us who the church's true teacher is. Paul, Apollos and Cephas are given to the church by Christ, as in Ephesians 4:11-12, but He alone is the Lord to whom the church answers.

Finally, the cross sits behind the whole argument. The wisdom that the Corinthians must unlearn, 'become a fool,' verse 18, is the wisdom of 1:18 to 2:16, the foolishness of the cross. The only way to become wise is to come to the crucified Christ and to build on Him.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is the one who gives growth. Paul's argument that 'neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow,' verse 7, is a claim about the work of God in the church. The change of a heart and the building of a congregation are not the product of technique. God is the author of the harvest. The unusual mix of tenses in verse 6 suggests that He is constantly at work. This should free preachers from both pride and despair: they are not responsible for the result, and no result is outside His hand.

God is also the owner. The word 'God's' falls on the field, the building, the fellow workers and the temple. The church is a possession, not a venture. Yet the ownership is not that of a landlord who is distant. It is the ownership of a God who lives in what He owns. 'God's Spirit dwells in you,' verse 16. The doctrine of God that Paul assumes here is of a Father, a Son and a Spirit who are present in the congregation. God has made His home among the Corinthians, divided and immature as they are.

The passage shows God's holiness. 'God's temple is holy,' verse 17, and the warning about destroying it is serious. A holy God does not treat the harming of His people as a small thing. He also cares about the quality of what is built in His name, and He will test it by fire. That is a sober word for every teacher and leader, and it is a word about the God who sees and judges all work.

The passage shows God's mercy as well. The man whose work burns is still saved, verse 15. The same God who tests also rescues. The warning and the rescue are not at odds, because both depend on the character of the one who laid the foundation. He does not abandon the one who built on it.

God is wise in a way that makes human wisdom look small. 'He catches the wise in their craftiness,' verse 19, and 'The LORD knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile,' verse 20. The God who knows all thoughts is not impressed by cleverness. He does not need a counsellor.

The practical result is worship. If God is the one who grows the field, owns the building and lives in the temple, then the only fitting response is to give Him the glory. The final verses add that this God is generous. 'All things are yours,' verse 21, because the one who owns everything has given Himself in Christ. Romans 8:32 asks, 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?' That is the God who is the Lord of this church.

crossReferences.note: The LORD plants a vineyard on a fertile hillside, tends it, and looks for fruit. Israel is the field in this song, and the whole picture is of God as the owner and cultivator. When Paul says 'you are God's field,' he is taking over the language of Israel's identity and applying it to a church of Jews and Gentiles.

'Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain.' Paul's claim that neither planter nor waterer is anything is a New Testament form of this old confession. Labour matters, but only because God is the real builder.

God lays a tested stone in Zion, a precious cornerstone and sure foundation, and whoever believes will not be shaken. Paul's foundation, the one already laid, is the same thought, and Peter applies this verse to Christ in 1 Peter 2:6. It shows that the foundation of the church is God's own act, and a person.

David lists gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and costly stones that he has provided for the house of God. Paul's list of building materials in verse 12 echoes the temple's costly materials, so that work done on Christ's foundation is measured against a temple standard.

The Lord comes like a refiner's fire and a launderer's soap, purifying the sons of Levi like gold and silver. The fire in 1 Corinthians 3:13 belongs to the same tradition. Fire in the Bible is not only destruction but the means by which God separates the genuine from the worthless.

Joshua the high priest is 'a firebrand snatched from the fire,' a man rescued from judgment by God's choice. It is the closest Old Testament image to Paul's man who is saved 'only as if through the flames.' Both texts show salvation as rescue, not achievement.

The household of God is built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as cornerstone, and grows into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit. This passage gathers foundation, building and temple into a single sentence, and shows that Paul keeps the pictures together elsewhere.

'We are the temple of the living God,' with God's promise to dwell with His people and walk among them. Paul uses the temple image again to urge holiness and separation from idols. It confirms that for Paul the temple is the community and that its holiness is something to be guarded.

Christ the living stone is rejected by men but precious to God, and believers are like living stones built into a spiritual house. Peter's picture shows that the foundation and the building are of the same kind: the church is made of the same living material as the stone it rests on.

'He catches the wise in their craftiness.' Paul quotes this in verse 19 as a Scripture proof that the world's wisdom is folly with God. The line comes from the mouth of Eliphaz, whom God later says did not speak rightly, Job 42:7, so the quotation is an example of a true statement within a flawed speech.

'The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile.' Paul changes 'man' to 'the wise' to apply it to the Corinthians' pride in learning. The Psalm sets God's knowledge against human schemes, and Paul sets it against human ranking of teachers.

'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?' This is the ground of 'all things are yours' in 1 Corinthians 3:21. Everything the Corinthians were trying to gain through their favourite teachers is already given in Christ.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is the story of a God who wants to live with His people. In Eden He walked in the garden. The fall drove the man and woman out, and the rest of Genesis, Exodus and Kings is the story of God coming close again by degrees. He walked with Abraham, He dwelt in a tent among Israel in the wilderness, and He filled Solomon's temple with His glory. But the temple was a building in one place, and its priests could not make the people clean. The prophets saw that the glory had left, Ezekiel 10, and that the building would be destroyed.

The prophets also saw a new thing. Ezekiel saw God's Spirit put within His people, Ezekiel 36:27, and a new temple from which life flowed, Ezekiel 47. Jeremiah saw a new covenant written on hearts. Paul's claim in chapter 3 is that this is happening. Gentile and Jewish believers in a Greek city are the place where God lives. The church is not a club that gathers around a leader. It is the temple of the Holy Spirit.

The passage also fits the earlier story in the image of the field. Israel had been God's vineyard, but the fruit was bad, Isaiah 5. The church is the new field in which God is making something grow, because the seed is the gospel and the growth is His. The foundation is the stone He laid in Zion. The whole story of Scripture narrows toward Christ and then widens again in the church, as the nations come into the building.

The warning of verses 12 to 17 looks back as well. Throughout the story, God's holy presence is dangerous to those who treat it lightly, from the death of Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus 10, to Ananias and Sapphira, Acts 5. Paul keeps the same note and says that division within the community is a form of that danger. But the Day also looks forward. The fire that tests the work is the fire of the last day, the day on which the Lord brings everything to light.

The story ends in a city without a temple building. In Revelation 21:22 John says, 'I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.' The picture is the final form of what Paul describes. The building is finished, the foundation is Christ, the materials are His people, and God lives with them forever. The Corinthians were a very imperfect early stage of that city, and Paul tells them to build, and to belong, as though they already stood in it.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call the Corinthians infants in Christ?

options.text: Their jealousy and party spirit show they are still spiritually immature.
options.note: Verse 3 links their worldliness to jealousy and dissension.

options.text: They had only recently been converted and needed time.
options.note: Newness plays a part, but Paul's point is their persisting immaturity shown in strife.

options.text: They lacked the intelligence to grasp deep teaching.
options.note: The issue is not intellect but worldliness and division.

options.text: They were never truly converted at all.
options.note: Paul still calls them brothers in Christ, though immature.

quiz.q: What is Paul's main point in the image of planting and watering?

options.text: Leaders are only servants; God alone gives the growth.
options.note: Verses 6 and 7 make God the one who makes things grow.

options.text: Paul deserves more honour because he planted first.
options.note: The opposite; neither planter nor waterer is anything before God.

options.text: The Corinthians should choose the best teacher to follow.
options.note: The whole point undercuts choosing sides among servants.

options.text: Church growth depends entirely on human effort.
options.note: Paul says only God, who makes things grow, is anything.

quiz.q: What is the one foundation of the church?

options.text: Jesus Christ, the only foundation that can be laid.
options.note: Verse 11 says no other foundation can be laid than Jesus Christ.

options.text: The teaching of the apostles as a whole.
options.note: The apostles build, but the foundation itself is Christ.

options.text: The unity and good works of the congregation.
options.note: These matter, but they are not the foundation, which is Christ alone.

options.text: Whichever leader a believer chooses to follow.
options.note: This is precisely the error Paul is correcting.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the church is God's temple?

options.text: God's Spirit dwells in the gathered people, who are holy and must not be destroyed.
options.note: Verses 16 and 17 make the church the dwelling of the Spirit.

options.text: The church building itself is sacred space.
options.note: The temple here is the people, not a physical structure.

options.text: Only especially devout members are the temple.
options.note: Paul addresses the whole church, you yourselves, as the temple.

options.text: The temple language is only a loose figure of speech.
options.note: Paul treats it seriously: destroying this temple brings God's judgment.

quiz.q: Why should the Corinthians stop boasting in men?

options.text: Because all things are already theirs, and they belong to Christ.
options.note: Verses 21 to 23 dissolve boasting: all things are yours, and you are Christ's.

options.text: Because boasting is simply bad manners.
options.note: True enough, but Paul's reason is far deeper: everything is already theirs in Christ.

options.text: Because only Paul deserves their loyalty.
options.note: Paul refuses such loyalty; he is only a servant.

options.text: Because leaders do not matter to the church at all.
options.note: Leaders matter as servants; the point is not to boast in them.

questions: Paul measures maturity not by knowledge but by whether jealousy and division mark our life. Where might that same test expose immaturity in you?
God alone gives the growth. How does that free you from both pride when ministry flourishes and despair when it seems fruitless?
There is only one foundation, Jesus Christ. What are you tempted to build your life or your church upon instead of Him?
Your work for Christ will one day be tested by fire. What would it change this week to build with gold rather than straw?
You are God's temple, the dwelling of His Spirit. How does knowing that the Spirit lives in the gathered church shape the way you treat other believers?
All things are yours, and you belong to Christ. Where are you grasping for something that is already yours in Him?

translationNotes.note: The phrase rendered God's fellow workers means workers who belong to God and labour in His service, not workers on the same level as God; the surrounding verses stress that God alone gives the growth.

Saved, but only as if through the flames pictures a man escaping a burning house with his life but nothing else; it affirms salvation by grace while the worthless work is lost, and does not teach a purgatory.
You yourselves are God's temple uses a plural you with a singular temple: the whole gathered church together is the one dwelling of the Spirit, not merely each believer individually.
